rows.why: The customer-facing application's intended purpose, the public users and settings it serves, and the harm it could do to customers are understood and documented.
Requirements for the customer-facing application (privacy of customers, safe answers, abuse resistance) are elicited and built into its design.
What the customer-facing AI does not know or must not answer is documented and told to customers and staff.
The benefits to customers of the customer-facing AI are examined and documented so they can be weighed against the harms of wrong or leaked answers.
The scope of what the customer-facing application may answer or do is specified and limited to what its capability and context support.
Human oversight of the customer-facing AI (review, escalation to a person, override) is defined, assessed and documented.
Likelihood, magnitude and cost of harm from public attacks and bad or leaked answers reaching customers are assessed from expected use and past incidents.
Answer quality and safety of the customer-facing application are measured under conditions like real customer use, not only in the lab.
The customer-facing application's behaviour in production is monitored for wrong answers, abuse patterns and drift.
The customer-facing AI is shown to give valid, reliable answers, and the conditions beyond which its answers cannot be relied on are documented.
The customer-facing AI is tested for unsafe or harmful answers and shown to fail safely when pushed beyond its limits.
Security of the public-facing AI against prompt injection, jailbreaks and abuse is tested, for example by red-teaming, and results are documented.
Customer interactions with the AI are logged with enough detail to review errors, abuse and leaks and to hold someone accountable.
Privacy risk of the customer-facing AI, including leaking one customer's or the organisation's data in answers, is examined and documented.
Customers can report problems with the AI's answers and appeal outcomes, and this feedback feeds the evaluation of the application.
A determination is made, using monitoring and test results, whether the customer-facing AI meets its purpose and should stay in front of customers.
Controls on the customer-facing AI (input and output filtering, guardrails, rate limits, data minimisation) are in place and applied to sustain its safe operation.
Procedures exist and are followed to respond to and recover from a new attack or harmful behaviour of the customer-facing AI once found.
The customer-facing AI can be quickly disabled or replaced by a fallback when it behaves outside intended use, and someone is responsible for doing so.
Incidents and errors from the customer-facing AI are communicated to affected customers and partners, tracked, and reviewed after recovery.

review.reason: Repeats MAP 2.2 (documented limits beyond which answers cannot be relied on), and answer validity and reliability with no attacker belongs to the Output area.
Scope of what the application may answer or do largely repeats MAP 2.2 (what it must not answer, told to customers); merge into one check or separate clearly.

Outcome is sustaining the value of the deployed system, but the why lists security controls (filtering, rate limits, data minimisation) that belong to Input/Output/Hosting; it does not ask how value is kept up (maintenance, updates, re-checks).

Folded MAP 5.2 is not fully asked: the why covers problem reports and appeals but not the practices and people for regular engagement or feedback on positive and unanticipated impacts; ask it fully or make MAP 5.2 its own row.
An assessor can ask whether answers given to customers are checked for bias or unequal treatment of different customers or groups; nothing in the draft covers it.
